title: Doing HAI Research
subtitle: Reading, experiments, statistics, qualitative methods, systems, your first study
overview: This stage turns readers into researchers and can run alongside any other. It covers reading papers and judging contributions, designing and analyzing experiments honestly, qualitative and design methods, evaluating systems, and planning your own HAI study, ending in a capstone study plan.

modules.title: Reading and thinking like a researcher
modules.goal: Read papers in deliberate passes, classify the kind of contribution each makes, and explain how researchers choose problems worth working on.
modules.guide: Start with Keshav's three-pass method; apply it immediately. Carey et al. add habits for goals, figures, and fair critique. Wobbrock & Kientz classify contributions, which tells you what evidence a paper owes. End with Hamming's talk on choosing important problems (transcript and 1995 video are separate deliveries). Key terms: 'contribution' (new knowledge or capability added); 'literature survey' (structured reading to map a field); 'related work' (positioning against prior research).

resources.title: How to read a paper
resources.why: A practical method for reading papers in passes, and for using it in a literature survey.
resources.focus: Read the whole thing (two pages), then apply it to the next paper you open.

resources.title: Ten simple rules for reading a scientific paper
resources.why: Adds student habits: set a reading goal, find the author's goal, unpack figures, be critical and kind.
resources.focus: Read all ten rules, especially those on figures and on being critical.

resources.title: Research contributions in human-computer interaction
resources.why: Defines the main HCI contribution types, which tell you how to evaluate a paper and frame your own.
resources.focus: Learn the seven contribution types and the example of how each is evaluated.

resources.title: You and Your Research
resources.why: A Bell Labs scientist's talk on doing important work: important problems, courage, open doors, and selling results.
resources.focus: Read the talk; the question-and-answer section at the end is optional.

resources.title: Hamming, "You and Your Research" (June 6, 1995)
resources.why: A later recorded delivery of the same talk, if you prefer to hear Hamming himself.

quiz.q: In Keshav's method, what does the first pass consist of?
choices: Reading every section carefully and checking the math
A five-to-ten-minute scan of the title, abstract, introduction, headings and conclusions, and a glance at the references
Re-implementing the paper from scratch
Reading only the figures
quiz.explain: Keshav's first pass is a quick bird's-eye scan of about five to ten minutes, after which you decide whether to read further. The second pass (up to an hour) grasps the content; the third pass goes into depth.

quiz.q: After a first pass, Keshav says you should be able to answer 'the five Cs'. Which of these is NOT one of them?
choices: Category
Correctness
Contributions
Complexity
quiz.explain: The five Cs are Category, Context, Correctness, Contributions and Clarity. Complexity is not one of them.

quiz.q: According to Keshav, what is the key to the third pass?
choices: Attempting to virtually re-implement the paper, making the same assumptions as the authors
Reading the paper aloud to a colleague
Counting citations to judge importance
Skipping straight to the conclusion
quiz.explain: The third pass tries to recreate the work under the authors' assumptions. Comparing your reconstruction with the paper reveals both its innovations and its hidden failings and assumptions.

quiz.q: Carey et al.'s first rule is to do what before reading?
choices: Read the paper's reviews
Email the authors
Pick your reading goal
Memorize the abstract
quiz.explain: Rule 1 is to pick your reading goal, since reading for general awareness, for a specific method, or for review calls for different depth. Later rules include understanding the author's goal, unpacking figures, and being both critical and kind.

quiz.q: In Wobbrock & Kientz's framework, a paper that introduces and validates a new questionnaire for measuring trust in AI makes mainly what type of contribution?
choices: Artifact
Methodological
Opinion
Survey
quiz.explain: A new or improved way of doing research or measuring something is a methodological contribution. An artifact contribution is a new system or technique; a survey contribution reviews a body of work; an opinion contribution argues a position.

quiz.q: A paper presents a new LLM-powered writing interface and shows several example uses. In Wobbrock & Kientz's terms, what is its primary contribution type?
choices: Theoretical
Dataset
Artifact
Empirical
quiz.explain: New systems, tools and interaction techniques are artifact contributions. An empirical contribution is new knowledge from studies of people; many papers combine types, but naming the primary one tells reviewers what evidence to expect.

quiz.q: What does Hamming observe about people who work with their office door closed?
choices: They do more important work in the long run
They are less productive day to day
They have more collaborators
They get more done in the short term but over years often end up working on slightly the wrong problems
quiz.explain: Hamming says closed-door workers are more productive today and tomorrow, but those who work with the door open tend to ultimately do important things, because contact with others tells them which problems matter.

modules.exercise: Take one HAI paper you have already read in this app (for example, Bansal et al. on complementarity, or Bastani et al. on learning). (1) Do a strict first pass and write the five Cs in one line each. (2) Name its primary and secondary contribution types in Wobbrock & Kientz's terms and say what evidence each type owes the reader. (3) Unpack its most important figure following Carey et al.: what is on each axis, what comparison it makes, and what it does not show. (4) Write three questions you would ask the authors. (5) Following Hamming, write down three problems you think are important in HAI right now, and for each, one reason it is not yet being attacked.

modules.title: Experiments and statistics
modules.goal: Explain effect size, statistical power, the limits of p-values, preregistration, and the main data-quality risks of crowdsourced studies.
modules.guide: In order: Cohen (power), Kaptein & Robertson (CHI statistics problems), Dragicevic (estimation over significance), Cockburn, Gutwin & Dix (preregistration), Kittur, Chi & Suh (crowdsourced data quality). Key terms: 'effect size' (difference size, e.g., Cohen's d); 'power' (chance of detecting a real effect); 'p-value' (probability of data this extreme if the null holds, not of the null); 'confidence interval' (plausible effect range); 'between-' vs 'within-subjects' (one vs all conditions per person).

resources.title: A power primer
resources.why: The classic short introduction to power analysis and the small, medium, and large effect-size conventions.
resources.focus: Read the four quantities (significance level, power, effect size, sample size) and the sample-size table.

resources.title: Rethinking statistical analysis methods for CHI
resources.why: Critiques significance testing in CHI papers, naming three recurring problems and urging focus on effect size and importance.
resources.focus: Read the three problems and the worked example using CHI data; skim the Bayesian discussion.

resources.title: Fair Statistical Communication in HCI
resources.venue: Modern Statistical Methods for HCI (Springer HCI Series)
resources.why: Argues for estimation (effect sizes with confidence intervals) and nuanced reporting over dichotomous significance claims.
resources.focus: Read the arguments against dichotomous thinking and the guidance on reporting and plotting confidence intervals.

resources.title: HARK No More: On the Preregistration of CHI Experiments
resources.why: Explains publication bias, HARKing, and the replication crisis for HCI, and argues for preregistration at CHI.
resources.focus: Read the sections on publication bias, HARKing, and low replication, and how preregistration addresses them.

resources.title: Crowdsourcing user studies with Mechanical Turk
resources.why: An early study of getting valid data from crowdworkers; its design advice still applies to online HAI studies.
resources.focus: Compare the two experiments and the design changes between them; read the design recommendations.

quiz.q: In Cohen's conventions for the standardized mean difference d, what value counts as a 'medium' effect?
quiz.explain: Cohen's conventions are d = 0.2 (small), 0.5 (medium) and 0.8 (large). He presented them as rough guides for when no better basis exists, not as universal standards.

quiz.q: What level of statistical power does Cohen's primer propose as a conventional target?
quiz.explain: Cohen proposes power of .80, meaning an 80% chance of detecting a true effect of the assumed size, alongside a significance level of .05. Power of .50 is a coin flip; .05 is the usual significance level, not a power target.

quiz.q: Kaptein & Robertson describe 'the fallacy of the transposed conditional'. What mistake is that?
choices: Using a one-tailed test instead of a two-tailed test
Reporting means instead of medians
Running too many conditions
Treating the p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data
quiz.explain: A p-value is the probability of the data (or more extreme) given the null hypothesis, not the probability of the null given the data. Kaptein & Robertson list this, neglect of power, and reluctance to interpret effect sizes as the three problems.

quiz.q: What does Dragicevic recommend in place of declaring results simply 'significant' or 'not significant'?
choices: Reporting only p-values to three decimals
Reporting effect sizes with confidence intervals and interpreting them with nuance
Avoiding statistics entirely
Using a stricter threshold such as p < .001
quiz.explain: Dragicevic argues for estimation: show how big the effect is and how uncertain, typically with confidence intervals, and avoid dichotomous conclusions. A stricter threshold keeps the same yes/no thinking.

quiz.q: What does 'HARKing' mean in Cockburn, Gutwin & Dix?
choices: Hiring Additional Research Knowledge workers
Halting A study when Results look Known
Hypothesizing After the Results are Known, then presenting the hypothesis as if it had been made in advance
Holding All Results until Key findings appear
quiz.explain: HARKing is presenting a hypothesis formed after seeing the data as if it had been predicted. It makes exploratory findings look confirmatory and inflates false positives; preregistration makes the difference visible.

quiz.q: What does preregistering an experiment accomplish?
choices: It records hypotheses and the analysis plan before data collection, so confirmatory and exploratory analyses can be told apart
It guarantees the results will be significant
It replaces the need for ethics approval
It prevents any exploratory analysis from being reported
quiz.explain: Preregistration time-stamps your predictions and plan. You can still report exploratory analyses; they are just labelled as such. It does not guarantee results or replace ethics review.

quiz.q: In Kittur, Chi & Suh's Mechanical Turk studies of rating Wikipedia articles, what change improved data quality in the second experiment?
choices: Paying workers ten times more
Adding explicitly verifiable questions so that answering in bad faith took about as much effort as answering honestly
Recruiting only workers from one country
Removing all open-ended questions
quiz.explain: The redesigned task asked verifiable, quantitative questions about each article before the subjective rating, which reduced gaming and brought ratings closer to experts'. The general lesson: design tasks so that honest effort is the easiest path.

modules.exercise: You plan an online between-subjects experiment comparing an AI decision aid with and without explanations, measuring accuracy. (1) Using Cohen's table or a power calculator, state the sample size per group needed to detect d = 0.5 with power .80 at alpha .05, and explain how it changes if you expect only d = 0.2. (2) Explain why a within-subjects design would need fewer participants, and what it would risk. (3) Write the one-sentence confirmatory hypothesis you would preregister and one exploratory question you would label as exploratory. (4) Following Dragicevic, sketch how you would report the main result (an estimate with a confidence interval, not just p). (5) Following Kittur et al., add two task-design features that make low-effort crowd responses detectable or less likely, such as attention checks with verifiable answers.

modules.title: Qualitative and design methods
modules.goal: Explain thematic analysis, when inter-rater reliability is appropriate, how design artifacts produce knowledge, and how Wizard of Oz studies simulate future systems.
modules.guide: Read Braun & Clarke first (thematic analysis, six phases). Then McDonald, Schoenebeck & Forte on whether to compute IRR; Zimmerman, Forlizzi & Evenson on research through design; and Dahlbäck, Jönsson & Ahrenberg on Wizard of Oz studies. Key terms: 'coding' (tagging data segments); 'theme' (shared pattern of meaning); 'IRR' (consistency across coders); 'research through design' (making things to produce knowledge); 'Wizard of Oz' (hidden human runs a seemingly automated system).

resources.title: Using thematic analysis in psychology
resources.why: The standard reference for thematic analysis, the most common way HAI papers analyze interviews and open-ended answers.
resources.focus: Read the key decisions (inductive vs theoretical, semantic vs latent) and six phases; skim pitfalls.

resources.title: Reliability and Inter-rater Reliability in Qualitative Research
resources.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
resources.why: Reviews how CSCW and HCI papers establish qualitative reliability, and when computing IRR makes sense.
resources.focus: Read findings on current norms and the guidelines on when IRR fits.

resources.title: Research through design as a method for interaction design research in HCI
resources.why: Shows how design practice produces research knowledge and offers criteria for judging such work.
resources.focus: Read how design research relates to engineers, behavioral scientists, and anthropologists, and the four evaluation criteria.

resources.title: Wizard of Oz studies — why and how
resources.why: A methods paper on simulating natural language interfaces with a hidden human operator, newly relevant to LLM research.
resources.focus: Read why simulation matters (people talk differently to computers) and advice on realistic, consistent simulation.

quiz.q: Which sequence matches Braun & Clarke's six phases of thematic analysis?
choices: Generate themes, collect data, code, write up, review, define
Write up, define themes, generate codes, familiarize, review, search
Code, compute inter-rater reliability, count themes, report frequencies, test, publish
Familiarize with the data, generate initial codes, search for themes, review themes, define and name themes, produce the report
quiz.explain: Braun & Clarke's phases run from familiarizing yourself with the data through coding, searching for themes, reviewing them, defining and naming them, and producing the report. They stress the process is recursive, moving back and forth between phases.

quiz.q: Braun & Clarke criticize describing themes as 'emerging' from data. Why?
choices: It hides the researcher's active role in identifying and selecting themes
Themes should always be decided before data collection
Themes only exist in quantitative data
Journals forbid the word
quiz.explain: Saying themes 'emerge' implies they sit in the data waiting to be found. Braun & Clarke emphasize that researchers actively identify, select and report themes, and should be explicit about the choices they made.

quiz.q: In Braun & Clarke's terms, what distinguishes a latent theme from a semantic theme?
choices: Latent themes are found by software; semantic themes by people
Latent themes appear only in the final phase
Latent themes go beyond what participants explicitly said to the underlying ideas and assumptions
Latent themes are those mentioned by most participants
quiz.explain: Semantic themes stay at the surface meaning of what was said; latent themes interpret underlying ideas, assumptions and conceptualizations. Prevalence (how many participants mention it) is a separate question.

quiz.q: What did McDonald, Schoenebeck & Forte find about how often CSCW and HCI qualitative papers report inter-rater reliability?
choices: Almost every qualitative paper reports it
It is rare, in around one in nine qualitative papers
It is required by the ACM
No paper had ever reported it
quiz.explain: In their sample of CSCW and HCI papers from 2016–2018, IRR appeared in about 1/9 of qualitative papers; authors used many other ways to communicate reliability.

quiz.q: A single researcher writes an auto-ethnography of using an AI companion for six months. Following McDonald et al., what is the most sensible view of IRR here?
choices: IRR is mandatory and should be computed with two random coders
IRR should be computed between the researcher's first and second readings
The paper should be converted into a survey study
IRR is likely not appropriate, because the analysis rests on one person's situated interpretation; reliability is better communicated in other ways
quiz.explain: McDonald et al. argue that whether IRR makes sense depends on the method and its epistemology. For interpretive approaches such as auto-ethnography, agreement statistics do not fit; transparency about process and reflexivity serve better.

quiz.q: Zimmerman, Forlizzi & Evenson propose criteria for evaluating research through design. Which is NOT one of their criteria?
choices: Invention
Relevance
Statistical significance
Extensibility
quiz.explain: Their four criteria are process, invention, relevance and extensibility. Design research is not judged by statistical significance; it is judged by whether the process is documented, the artifact is novel, it matters, and others can build on it.

quiz.q: Why might an HAI researcher choose a Wizard of Oz study instead of using a real LLM?
choices: Wizard of Oz studies need no ethics review
To control exactly what the 'AI' says, for example to make it wrong on specific trials, or to test behavior no current system can produce
Because participants always prefer human operators
Because LLMs cannot be used in research
quiz.explain: Dahlbäck et al. motivate Wizard of Oz as a way to study how people interact with a system before it exists. In HAI it also gives experimental control over the AI's behavior. Because participants are misled about the system, ethics review and debriefing are still needed.

modules.exercise: Plan a small qualitative study: interviews with 10 knowledge workers about when they stop checking AI outputs. (1) Write five interview questions that ask for specific recent episodes rather than general opinions. (2) Decide whether your thematic analysis will be inductive or theoretical (for example, framed by the trust-calibration literature) and justify it. (3) Describe your coding process with a collaborator and decide, following McDonald et al., whether you will compute IRR and why. (4) Propose one Wizard of Oz probe to add to the interviews, such as a simulated assistant whose errors you control, and describe how you would debrief participants. (5) Note one way a research-through-design artifact (for example, a provocative 'checking nudge' prototype) could extend the study.

modules.title: Building and evaluating systems
modules.goal: Explain why standard usability tests are often the wrong evaluation for new systems and toolkits, and which alternative claims and strategies HCI accepts.
modules.guide: Many HAI contributions are systems: interfaces, toolkits, or research platforms. Read Olsen first on the distinct claims systems research makes, then Greenberg & Buxton on how premature or ill-fitting evaluation harms good ideas, then Ledo et al. on how toolkits are evaluated. Key terms: 'toolkit' (software for building interfaces); 'ecological validity' (match to real use); 'existence proof' (building something proves it possible); 'expressive leverage' (doing more while specifying less).

resources.title: Evaluating user interface systems research
resources.why: Offers claims (importance, generality, viscosity, expressive leverage, scalability) for evaluating UI systems on their own terms.
resources.focus: Read the critique of usability testing for systems and how to support each claim.

resources.title: Usability evaluation considered harmful (some of the time)
resources.why: Argues that reflexive usability evaluation can stifle novel ideas, and that methods should fit the research question.
resources.focus: Read the main argument and the cases where usability evaluation is inappropriate or misleading.

resources.title: Evaluation Strategies for HCI Toolkit Research
resources.authors: Ledo, Houben, Vermeulen, Marquardt, Oehlberg, Greenberg
resources.why: Organizes how toolkit papers are evaluated into four strategies with pitfalls; useful if you build AI interface tools.
resources.focus: Read the four evaluation strategies and the pitfalls listed for each.

quiz.q: Olsen argues usability testing often fits UI systems research poorly. Which assumption behind usability testing does he criticize?
choices: That participants are paid
That systems are open source
That the system is walk-up-and-use, tasks are standardized, and the problem is small enough to test in a session
That evaluations use statistics
quiz.explain: Olsen identifies the walk-up-and-use assumption, the standardized-task assumption, and the scale-of-problem assumption. Toolkits and complex systems typically require expertise, open-ended tasks, and long use, so a short usability session cannot capture their value.

quiz.q: Olsen asks systems researchers to state the importance of their work in terms of 'STU'. What does STU stand for?
choices: Situations, Tasks, Users
Speed, Throughput, Usability
Systems, Tools, Utilities
Study, Test, Update
quiz.explain: STU stands for Situations, Tasks and Users: the population, the tasks they need to do, and the situations in which they do them. Importance claims should say which STU contexts the system improves.

quiz.q: In Olsen's vocabulary, what does it mean for a tool to have 'expressive leverage'?
choices: It runs faster than previous tools
It is easier for beginners to learn
It is compatible with many programming languages
A designer can accomplish more by expressing less
quiz.explain: Expressive leverage means a designer gets more done with fewer choices or less specification, for example by reusing common patterns. Olsen pairs it with expressive match: how closely the tool's way of expressing designs matches the problem.

quiz.q: What is Greenberg & Buxton's main concern about usability evaluation?
choices: It is always too expensive
Applied reflexively or too early, it can kill novel ideas and lead to weak science when the method does not fit the question
It should be replaced entirely by surveys
It overestimates how much users like new systems
quiz.explain: Greenberg & Buxton do not reject usability evaluation; they argue it is harmful some of the time, particularly for early-stage inventions, and that the evaluation method should follow from the research question.

quiz.q: Ledo et al. organize toolkit evaluations into four strategies. Which is NOT one of them?
choices: Demonstration
Usage
Market adoption
Technical performance
quiz.explain: The four strategies are demonstration, usage, technical performance, and heuristics. Long-term adoption can be strong evidence, but it is not one of the four categories they define.

quiz.q: You built a toolkit that lets researchers create Wizard of Oz HAI experiments with configurable AI errors. Which first evaluation best matches Ledo et al.'s 'demonstration' strategy?
choices: Building several example studies with the toolkit that would previously have been hard to build, to show breadth
A 10-minute usability test with first-time users
Measuring how fast the toolkit loads
Counting GitHub stars after a week
quiz.explain: Demonstration shows what the toolkit makes possible through examples, often novel or replicated ones. Load time is technical performance; a short walk-up test is a usage evaluation with exactly the limits Olsen warns about.

modules.exercise: Imagine you have built 'TrustLens', a toolkit that lets designers add calibrated-uncertainty displays to any LLM interface. (1) State two of Olsen's claims you would make (for example, reducing solution viscosity or expressive leverage) and what evidence would support each. (2) Choose two of Ledo et al.'s strategies and design one concrete evaluation for each. (3) Explain why, following Greenberg & Buxton, a standard 30-minute usability test with novices would be a poor primary evaluation. (4) Describe one follow-up empirical study, with real end users, that tests whether interfaces built with TrustLens actually improve reliance calibration.

modules.title: Capstone: your first HAI study
modules.goal: Produce a complete, defensible plan for a human-AI interaction experiment: question, hypotheses, design, measures, power, validity threats, and ethics.
modules.guide: The exercise is the main work. Use Lazar, Feng & Hochheiser for design, Hart for NASA-TLX workload, Jian, Bisantz & Drury for trust, and the HAX Toolkit for AI interface design. AsPredicted (optional) helps draft a preregistration. Key terms: 'independent variable' (what you manipulate); 'dependent variable' (what you measure); 'confound' (co-varying alternative explanation); 'counterbalancing' (varying condition order); 'internal' vs 'external validity' (sound causation vs generalization); 'IRB' (human-subjects ethics review).

resources.title: Experimental design (Chapter 3 of Research Methods in Human Computer Interaction, 2nd ed.)
resources.why: Covers between-subjects, within-subjects, and factorial designs and their tradeoffs: everything your plan's design section needs.
resources.focus: Read the between-group, within-group, and split-plot sections, plus learning effects and counterbalancing.

resources.title: Nasa-Task Load Index (NASA-TLX); 20 Years Later
resources.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
resources.why: The NASA-TLX creator's short review of how the workload questionnaire has been used and modified.
resources.focus: Note the six subscales and the common 'Raw TLX' simplification that drops pairwise weighting.

resources.title: Foundations for an Empirically Determined Scale of Trust in Automated Systems
resources.why: Develops a widely adapted trust-in-automation questionnaire; know its origins and what it measures before using it.
resources.focus: Read how items were derived and the final 12-item scale; note conclusions on trust and distrust.

resources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit
resources.why: Practical resources (patterns, workbook, failure playbook) built on the Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, for designing your AI condition.
resources.focus: Browse the guidelines and the playbook for planning how your AI will fail.

resources.title: AsPredicted
resources.why: A lightweight preregistration form with short questions on hypotheses, measures, conditions, analyses, exclusions, and sample size.
resources.focus: Read the form's questions and use them as a checklist for your study plan.

quiz.q: You compare two explanation designs within subjects: every participant uses design A for 20 trials, then design B for 20 trials. What is the most serious problem?
choices: Within-subjects designs need more participants than between-subjects designs
Order is confounded with design: practice, fatigue, or learning about the AI's errors in the A block could explain differences in B
Participants cannot rate two designs
There is no problem; this is the standard design
quiz.explain: Running A always before B means any order effect (learning, fatigue, or learning how reliable the AI is) is mixed up with the design difference. Lazar et al. discuss learning effects and counterbalancing for this reason. Within-subjects designs usually need fewer participants, not more.

quiz.q: Why do researchers counterbalance the order of conditions in a within-subjects study?
choices: To make the study shorter
To ensure every participant prefers the same condition
To remove the need for statistics
So that order effects are spread evenly across conditions and do not systematically favor one
quiz.explain: Counterbalancing (e.g., half the participants get A then B, half B then A, or a Latin square for more conditions) balances order effects across conditions so they do not bias the comparison.

quiz.q: A researcher runs the AI-assisted condition in morning sessions and the no-AI condition in evening sessions, and finds the AI group more accurate. What is the problem?
choices: Time of day is a confound: it varies with the condition and could explain the difference
The study lacks a dependent variable
The sample is too large
Accuracy cannot be measured in the evening
quiz.explain: Because time of day changes together with the condition, alertness or a different kind of participant who signs up for evening sessions could produce the difference. Random assignment of participants to conditions within each time slot removes this confound.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six NASA-TLX subscales?
choices: Mental demand
Frustration
Trust
Temporal demand
quiz.explain: The NASA-TLX subscales are mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort and frustration. Trust needs a separate instrument, such as Jian et al.'s scale.

quiz.q: What do Jian, Bisantz & Drury conclude about trust and distrust in automation, based on their scale development?
choices: Trust and distrust can be treated as opposite ends of a single dimension
Trust and distrust are completely unrelated
Distrust cannot be measured by questionnaire
Trust is the same as reliability
quiz.explain: Their analysis suggested trust and distrust behave as opposites on one dimension, which is why the final 12-item scale includes both trust items and distrust items on a single instrument rather than two separate scales.

quiz.q: Why should an HAI study measure behavioral reliance (for example, how often participants follow the AI when it is wrong) and not only a trust questionnaire?
choices: Questionnaires are not allowed in experiments
Behavioral measures never need statistics
Trust questionnaires measure workload instead
Stated trust and actual reliance can diverge, and appropriate reliance is usually the outcome that matters
quiz.explain: People can report low trust and still follow the AI, or the reverse. Measuring agreement with correct versus incorrect AI advice separates appropriate reliance from over- and under-reliance, which is the core outcome in the decision-making literature from earlier stages.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a small pilot study before the main experiment?
choices: To produce the paper's main result
To replace the power analysis entirely with the pilot's p-value
To find problems with the procedure, materials, timing and instructions before spending the full budget
To recruit participants for the main study
quiz.explain: Pilots catch confusing instructions, broken interfaces, ceiling or floor effects and timing problems. They can give rough estimates of variance, but effect sizes from tiny pilots are unreliable, so power analyses should not rest on a pilot's estimate alone.

modules.exercise:
Write a complete plan (about two pages) for a first HAI experiment. Use this running example or substitute your own: 'Does asking people to state their own answer before seeing an LLM's suggestion reduce overreliance on wrong suggestions?'

1. Research question and motivation: one paragraph citing two papers from earlier stages (for example, Buçinca et al. on cognitive forcing and Bansal et al. on complementarity).
2. Hypotheses: H1 about reliance on incorrect AI advice, H2 about overall accuracy, H3 about workload. Each must name the direction of the effect.
3. Design: independent variable(s) and levels (e.g., answer-first vs AI-first, plus a no-AI baseline); between- vs within-subjects, with your reasoning on carryover effects (learning the AI's error rate) vs sample size; how you will counterbalance if you go within-subjects.
4. Task and AI behavior: the task domain, number of trials, the AI's accuracy, and which trials it gets wrong. Explain why you control the AI's errors (scripted or Wizard of Oz) instead of using live LLM outputs, and use the HAX Toolkit to make the AI condition realistic.
5. Measures: behavioral reliance (agreement with AI when the AI is right vs wrong), accuracy, time, NASA-TLX (raw or weighted, and why), a trust scale (e.g., Jian et al.), plus one open-ended question for thematic analysis.
6. Power and pilot: the smallest effect size you care about and why, the sample size from a power analysis (Cohen), and what the pilot (5–10 people) will check.
7. Analysis plan: the confirmatory test for each hypothesis, the effect size and confidence interval you will report (Dragicevic), exclusion rules decided in advance (attention checks, Kittur et al.), and which analyses are exploratory. Draft it in the AsPredicted format.
8. Threats to validity: at least two internal (e.g., confounds, demand effects) and two external (e.g., crowdworkers vs professionals, low stakes vs real stakes), each with a mitigation.
9. Ethics and IRB: informed consent, any deception and debriefing, risks (e.g., exposure to wrong AI advice on sensitive topics), fair pay for crowdworkers, data privacy, and how participants can withdraw.
10. Expected contribution: in Wobbrock & Kientz's terms, what type it is and what a null result would still teach the field.
